column2: Brahma too, in a former kalpa, bestowing grace on the worlds — the linga named Madhyeshvara stands in the midst of the water;
it is worshipped by naga maidens and men do not see it. The Darukeshvara linga destroys all sins;
by worshipping that god a man becomes a vidyadhara. Then one should go to the Bhrigu linga, where Bhairava stands;
going to Bhrigu, best of men, one is freed from the sin of killing a brahmin. Then one should go to Jaleshvara, the very best of mountain holy places;
a man who merely bathes there is not born again in worldly existence; by giving sesame water the ancestors gain an imperishable goal.
Taking the form of Bhairava, Hara cast down Bana's three cities into the midst of the water of the Narmada
with the blazing Pashupata weapon right there; then, from the contact of that weapon, there quickly rose from the netherworld
the linga named Jaleshvara, which removes the sin of killing a brahmin. Then one should go to Kotitirtha and bathe according to rule,
and tie a white thread for Omkara, O Bharata; having worshipped Omkara, he should light a row of lamps:
The thread sacrifice is fruitful by your grace, Maheshvara. He should feed ascetics there and give fees according to his means,
and break his fast together with his kin and servants, O king. Whoever with bodily hardship walks around Shiva's mountain
gains the fruit of a sacrifice at every step, so Shankara said. Long ago, by all the hosts of gods, by siddhas, gandharvas and kinnaras,
by vidyadharas, yakshas, asuras, daityas and danavas, by the moon, sun and planets, by the circles of stars and the pole,
by the Vishvedevas, Sadhyas, Maruts and Vasus, by the king of the gods, by Indrani and Savitri, O Bharata,
by Arundhati, Sarasvati and Gayatri, that mountain was devoutly encircled with thread, and the fruit declared by Shiva was obtained.
Ahalya, Menaka, Rambha, Ghritachi and Urvashi, Tilottama and others, and the rivers and oceans too —
by encircling this mountain one attained the divinity of the quarters. As long as the moon and sun endure and the earth stands,
by the power of the thread sacrifice one dwells so long in Shiva's city. This I have told you, O king, the fruit of the thread sacrifice;
by hearing and reciting this, one becomes an attendant of Rudra.
In this region, best of kings, Kotitirtha is situated, with a hundred thousand holy places dwelling in the netherworld,
established by Shiva between the Kapila and the Narmada. Here, great king, having bathed according to rule in the water of Rudravarta,
they go to Shiva's abode. Those who dwell on the northern bank dwell in Rudra's world;
those who dwell on the left side go to Vishnu's world; those who dwell on the eastern and western sides at Amarakantaka
go to the world of Rudra, of Brahma and of Vishnu. By death in water eleven, in fire and in falling sixteen,
and likewise eighty thousand by death in a cowpen; by fasting, Brahma's world is declared for a lakh and a half.
Those who accomplish death by water or fire in the waters of the Kapila and Narmada dwell in Rudra's world for a thousand cycles of four ages.
Whether helplessly or willingly, beasts, birds and reptiles, sinful ones gone into animal births, who die here, Yudhishthira,
are born as kings in the auspicious city of the vidyadharas. At the conjunction of Rahu and Soma at Kotitirtha, lord of men,
the merit declared for men has no number. At Gaya, Kurukshetra, Pushkara and Amarakantaka
one obtains equal fruit when the sun is seized by Rahu. Where the eastward-flowing Sarasvati is, Sthanu and the Sarasvata water,
what is given there increases twelve and a half lakh times; all that is equal at Kotitirtha, no doubt,
for wealth lawfully gained, when the sun is seized by Rahu. Merit of many kinds has been declared in various views,
and what Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva have spoken is accepted by all as authority. Men of little strength, O king, deluded by maya in this age,
do not see Omkara and the Kalpaga of seven kalpas. Great king, the difference between a cow and a goat, between gold and silver,
between a shudra and a brahmin, between curd and buttermilk — such is the Amareshvara holy place to be known compared with other holy places.
Whatever gold is given at Kotitirtha, even the weight of a gunja seed, has no number until the dissolution.
Kotitirtha is four cubits in extent, no doubt; others say one cubit, others a span,
some four fingers, some a finger's breadth, half a finger, the size of a barley grain, the thickness of the sacred thread.
In the twenty-fourth twelve-year period, the Sarasvati, to bathe at Kotitirtha from Kurukshetra when the sun is seized by Rahu,
comes in the form of a she-elephant, from the diminishing of her own merit; having bathed, she returns to Kurukshetra, no doubt.
From the confluence of the Kaveri up to the confluence with the ocean, in this stretch, great king, ten crore holy places are remembered.
From Kotitirtha to the end of the Nilaganga there are eight lakh holy places, measured by the sacred thread;
and on the eastern side of the Kaveri up to the Paryanka mountain, ten lakh holy places — the number has been told you.
Reaching on the Narmada the great hermitage of Jamadagni, Shrikantha and Nilakantha, the linga that destroys sin,
Kanyatirtha of great merit, the excellent Kapileshvara, and the holy place called Kapilavarta, supreme remover of sin —
there Pushan, the sun, devoted to meditation on Shiva, practised most difficult austerity for a thousand divine years.
Then the lord of gods, pleased, said to him, O king: "Choose a boon — blessings on you — whatever is in your mind."
Pushan said: "If you are pleased, lord of gods, and wish to give a boon — the linga called Suryapingala, giving supreme success,
radiant in the sky like the thousand-rayed sun blazing with its rays; and each month let another Mitra transit through the other signs.
This I regard as the boon, which illumines the world." The Lord said: "Prosperity with all wealth will be yours by my grace."
In the Krita age, great king, I myself saw this. By worshipping Pingaleshvara on the fourteenth and eighth,
one gains the fruit of ten million sacrifices and is honoured in Shiva's world. The self-manifested gods on the banks of the Reva within a krosha
are all to be known as givers of success and of the fruits of desire and enjoyment; some are the size of a pumpkin, some the size of a flower,
some the size of a castor fruit, some of the size of a diamond or pearl. In the Krita age they are said to be of jewels, in the Treta of gold,
in the Dvapara of silver and copper, and in the Kali they are remembered as of stone. They call the Krita age brahmin, the Treta kshatriya,
the Dvapara vaishya and the Kali shudra likewise. No one who reaches the holy linga and dies at Amarakantaka —
who would not be freed, son of Kunti, from the sin of seven births? Such as this holy mountain Amarakantaka is on every side,
I see nothing like it in the three worlds, O Bharata. All around the mountain a crore of holy places stand;
reaching the stairway to heaven, one has the direct vision of Shiva. Most holy is Kotitirtha, and Amarakantaka likewise;
know them to give heaven and liberation and every success. Mandhatri was perfected on the Vaidurya mountain in the Krita age,
as has been told, tiger among kings; I shall tell you something else. The holy confluence of the Kaveri is renowned in all worlds;
those who bathe and die there go to heaven, free of rebirth. When vyatipata falls on a Tuesday with the fourteenth on the Kaveri,
the merit at her confluence becomes a thousandfold. Those slain by weapons, by the gift of water mixed with sesame
and by the ekoddishta shraddha, attain the world of heaven. Death at the hands of a chandala, a hunter, a serpent, lightning or even a brahmin,
by tusked beasts and animals — the deaths of sinners — all of them, tiger among kings, at the auspicious confluence of the Kaveri,
through the performance of shraddha truly go satisfied to the supreme goal. Kubera practised austerity there for a thousand divine years;
having worshipped and honoured the lord of the worlds, the husband of Uma, endowed with Shiva's grace he attained the guardianship of a world-quarter.
Hear the fruit of merit of one who gives up his life there: he attains the kingship of the gods for sixty thousand years.
Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly, is a king in the city of the vidyadharas for ten thousand years.
With the waters of the Reva and Kaveri and with wild sesame, the ancestors satisfied there go, content, to the supreme goal.
The Kaveri is spread over the earth with thousands of mouths; as the moving and unmoving world is pervaded by the wind and the rays of the sun,
so the surface of the earth is pervaded by the water of the Kaveri. On the southern bank of the Narmada, on the Varaha, a Vindhya mountain,
from which, visible to all the gods, the Payoshni came forth — she was the daughter of Soma, cool as the moon in the womb of snow,
once worshipped by Hara, abounding in water, in the form of Uma; for the deliverance of the worlds she is sung as the Somaganga.
She came forth from the body of the glorious Boar. Bathing there, O king, a man is not born again in worldly existence.
By his giving sesame water, O Bharata, his ancestors sport in Shankara's world for a hundred million years.
The fruit of bathing there on the full moon of Kartika, on the Varaha of the Vindhya, cannot be counted even in hundreds of years;
so Shiva told long ago in the Purana proclaimed by Skanda. The gift given there has no number.
Those who worship the Boar are not ordinary men; when they give up life there they attain Shiva's world.
At the conjunction of Rahu and Soma on the Varaha of the Vindhya, the merit equals that of Kurukshetra, so Shankara said long ago.
From the mountain Varaha to the confluence of the Payoshni, in this stretch, best of kings, a crore of holy places is declared.
At the confluence of the Payoshni there it is called Somavarta; that region is holy on every side — this truth I have told you.
At the sin-removing confluence of the Payoshni, by the sight of the linga — the bathing and giving there cannot be counted.
The meeting of the Tapi and Payoshni at eclipses of moon and sun, O king, is declared by Shiva a hundred times greater than Kurukshetra,
where the four-armed Hari, lord of Shri, supreme Person, dwells; it is to be known as a field of Vishnu, a krosha in extent, O king.
In the month of Ashvina, in the dark fortnight, the fourteenth, the new moon and Sinivali — these are the festival days in order.
On the fourteenth in the fourfold conjunction it flows with nectar, O king; the ancestors are satisfied on that day, no doubt.
Whatever fruit is declared at Kurukshetra at a solar eclipse, that fruit is declared at the meeting of the Tapi and Payoshni.
At the offering of lamps on the Kaumudi night the fruit is beyond counting; the man who offers a lamp there becomes an emperor.
In Kartika and Ashvina, in both fortnights — hear the fruit of merit of one who does not eat for a month:
as long as the moon, the sun, the Himalaya and the great ocean endure, so long he dwells in heaven and in Vishnu's world, O Bharata.
On the southern side of the Narmada, splitting the earth and rising from the netherworld, is what is renowned in the three worlds as the Kaveri pool;
a man who merely bathes there attains the leadership of ganas. Kundeshvara is a Siddhalinga frequented by gods and siddhas;
whoever even inadvertently worships that pure linga — the merit of it has no number as long as moon, sun and stars endure.
By giving sesame water and offering pindas, O Bharata, the satisfaction of the ancestors lasts countless ages, no doubt.
By the power of the Kaveri and her confluence with the Narmada, the region became Yajnavarta — this truth was spoken by Shiva.
There are self-manifested lingas that give heaven and liberation; a man who bathes anywhere there in the Kaveri, best of kings,
gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice and is honoured in Vishnu's world; giving up his life on the Kaveri he attains Kubera's world.
The Kubereshvara linga, which grants every success, lies between the Kaveri and Narmada, and men do not see it;
it is worshipped by gods and daityas and honoured by naga maidens; by worshipping that god, like the twelve suns,
freed from all sins, one is honoured in Shiva's world. At the meeting of the Kaveri and Narmada a bana linga is established,
seen long ago by Kubera, named Sangameshvara; by worshipping that god one dwells in the city of the world-guardians.
The fruit declared at the meeting of the Ganga and Yamuna on a Tuesday with the fourteenth, at vyatipata and at the solar transit,
and at the conjunction of Rahu and Soma, is remembered as eightfold here. Eighty merits are declared at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna;
at the meeting of the Kaveri and Narmada the banas are remembered as eightfold. It is worshipped by sixty thousand guardians of the field of the Ganga;
other holy places are guarded by half that number, no doubt. To the south of Amareshvara is the linga Jaleshvara;
by seeing that linga one attains the leadership of ganas. The Narmada of seven kalpas is guarded by gods in lakhs,
by sixty thousand archers, Yudhishthira; Omkara, the mountain and the linga by a hundred thousand.
Sin committed elsewhere is destroyed in a holy field; sin committed in a holy field becomes like a coating of diamond.
Through momentary hardship one attains supreme happiness.
Saudamini was his wife, his lawful and glorious wife, endowed with beauty and youth, radiant as moonlight,
lovely, wearing bark garments, with full, high breasts. I shall tell you the ancient story of her and of him.
Chandrasena, mounted on a horse, hunting deer in the forest, came to the hermitage of Shandilya, who dwelt in the Naimisha forest.
He then saw Saudamini, Shandilya's beloved, and said to her: "Be my queen.
Your husband wears bark and deerskin, has rings of kusha and kasha grass, lives on bulbs, roots and fruits — a brahmin.
What will you do with him? By my grace always enjoy my abundant pleasures, fair one."
Hearing those words of the sinful king, Saudamini said to Chandrasena, vilest of kings:
Ask my husband, O king; I am subject to him. The king said to Shandilya, "Then I choose her from you;
if this woman is your wife, give her to me today; I will give you a hundred thousand in wealth as her price."
Shandilya said: "All women have deceit at their root; there is none dear to them in the world of men. Do as you please, lord of the earth; why ask me, a weak brahmin?"
Then the king, blind with desire, seized her by the hand. She, looking at the wicked one, blazing with fierce anger, said: "I am in my season; having touched me, you will become a chandala."
Seeing his beloved thus, naked and stricken with fear, he became a chandala that very instant, a terror to all beings.
Then all the gods with men raised cries of lament. Mounting his horse, the king entered the city of Ayodhya.
Seeing him in chandala form, the brahmin citizens, the princes and those dwelling in the king's inner apartments
were stricken with fear and reproached the king. Grieving over his own body, he went to Vasishtha for refuge,
and the king, his face downcast, said to his family priest: "I went to the region of the Naimisha forest,
and having saluted Shandilya and prostrated with eight limbs, I said, 'Give me your wife for much wealth.'
In his presence I was cursed by Shandilya's wife." Hearing the account of that sinful king,
Vasishtha said to King Chandrasena: "Go, king of kings, to Shandilya, the ascetic who approaches his wife only in her season,
and to Saudamini, the sage's wife, blazing as if with radiance." Saying "So be it" and bowing to his priest,
he went to the region of the Naimisha forest, and bowing to Shandilya again and again with eight limbs,
the king, trembling with fear, said to that best of sages: "Forgive me, best of sages, who desired your wife.
You are my mother and father; uplift the line of Raghu. I have wronged you today, and have received its fruit."
The brahmin, pleased, and his chaste wife said: "Markandeya is my father, O king; I am the disciple of that wise one.
I came here to the Naimisha forest for the sake of a wife. But you go, best of kings, to the confluence of the Chandavega;
having worshipped Chandeshvara and bathed there, best of kings, you will attain the supreme place and be freed from this sin."
Hearing those words of the great-souled Shandilya, the king bowed to Shandilya and to Saudamini:
Blessings on you; I shall go to the confluence of the Chandavega. Having said this he went there, and arriving, the lord of the earth
worshipped Chandeshvara and bathed there according to rule; mounted on a divine vehicle, praised by hosts of apsarases,
freed from all sins by the power of this holy place, King Chandrasena reached Shiva's city in an instant.
When the Svarochisha Manvantara had come, in the first kalpa, in the Krita age, thousands of beings attained perfection there.
This I have told you, O king, of the confluence of the Chandavega; by hearing or reciting it the sin of killing an embryo perishes.
Anointing it with saffron, one should worship it with fragrance and incense; one rejoices in Shiva's presence for a thousand divine years.
By seeing that linga one attains the leadership of ganas. The linga named Bhadrarudreshvara gives supreme success.
In a former kalpa the two gandharva brothers Bhadra and Rudra worshipped it according to rule and went to the city of the vidyadharas.
The ancestors and grandsires sing a verse: by giving sesame water and offering pindas, O Bharata,
one dwells here in Rudra's world for fourteen Manvantaras. Men slain by weapons, or who died in sin by fate,
through the shraddha on the fourteenth and the release of a bull, O Bharata, attain the world of heroes and sport there.
Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly, by the power of this holy place is not born again in worldly existence;
he is a king in the city of the vidyadharas for a thousand cycles of four ages. I shall tell a story as it was seen long ago, sinless one.
When the Chakshusha Manvantara had come, in the first kalpa, in the Krita age, there was long ago a king named Nimi, an emperor, lord of the people,
who went into a bird's birth through the anger of a brahmin; by the greatness of this holy place, at the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday,
having bathed, he left that birth, ruled a kingdom and went to heaven. Yudhishthira said: How did that king obtain a human body again?
This seems a marvel to me; tell me, great-minded one. Markandeya said: Chyavana asked the king for a maiden named Sukanya.
Nimi had a chaste queen named Chandravati; she bore a daughter dearer to her than life.
Once the best of kings, sitting at ease, seeing Chyavana arrive by chance, honoured him with arghya and water for the feet:
Today my birth is fruitful from seeing your lotus feet; I regard this as a grace — please take a meal.
Hearing his words, the sage Chyavana said: "If you give me your maiden, devoted to dharma, as a wife,
then I will eat, lord of the earth; otherwise you will incur sin." The king said: "I have one daughter, O brahmin; ask the fair queen.
I am not able to give my daughter — I tell you truly." Then, hearing the king's words, the sage spoke to the queen:
Give me the maiden, queen, for the sake of a son for a householder. Laughing, the queen said: "She is not fit for you, best of brahmins;
ask for something else, brahmin sage, and I will give it without doubt." Then in anger he cursed her: "You will go into a bird's birth."
Hearing the curse, the queen then cursed the great sage: "If I have truth and unwavering devotion to my husband,
since I have been cursed without fault, you will become blind." Having cursed each other, the two came to the bank of the Narmada.
Chyavana practised fierce austerity at the confluence of the Erandi for a thousand divine years, covered by an anthill.
On the eastern side of the mountain is what is remembered as Madhyaranya; reaching a kadamba tree in that forest, the couple,
in the flowering and fruiting lovely tree, were born in the form of birds; other birds too were born there by the thousand,
remembering their births and speaking excellent human speech; those sarangas were birds ever joyful in heart.
When the month of Jyeshtha came, a forest fire burned the forest; all the egg-born perished, overwhelmed by garlands of flame.
Clinging to the hollow of the tree with their young at ease — once, O Bharata, the female bird there was with young.
The female bird said to her mate: "Why do you stay without fear? All the birds have gone; will you let us be destroyed?"
Hearing her words, the bird said: "How can I go alone, leaving my wife and sons, dear one?
This has never been seen anywhere by anyone, in the world or in the Veda. The wife taken by the hand, of good conduct and walking in dharma —
he who leaves her and goes out of delusion is declared a slayer of an embryo." The female bird said: "Protect yourself, lord of my life, the root of the family.
You will have other wives by the hundred thousand again. She who, while her husband lives, desires another man
is most sinful and wicked, and is born a worm in excrement. The widow bereft of her husband who does not follow her own husband,
even if she lives a hundred years, is declared most sinful. The woman who dies before her husband while he lives
goes to the supreme goal through the water-offerings and shraddha given by her husband. By whose grace sons, ornaments and fame are obtained —
who is dearer than he, here and hereafter? The forest fire has come of itself; go quickly. How can I leave my sons
and go, lord of my life? Destruction is upon us now; I have neither hands nor feet, and the fire does not abate.
Birds that live by eggs are unable to carry them. The mother who leaves her sons and goes, stricken with fear, is reproached;
she is surely born a she-serpent for seven births." Having said this there, of their sons, one by one,
gathering them with effort, pair by pair, the couple placed them at the Erandika confluence, and the husband said to his wife:
Our sons must be carefully protected from beasts of prey; I am going now to bring the other sons, dear one.
Having said this, the bird went to his dwelling in the kadamba tree; he saw then that the dwelling there was full of fire.
Out of love, seeking his sons, he entered the house surrounded by garlands of flame; then the fire burned him with his sons and the tree.
Burned by that fire, he became like a heap of fire. When that forest had been reduced to ashes, the rainy season came,
and there everything was washed into the water of the Erandi, O king. At the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday, that bird's bones
by fate reached the confluence of the Erandi, best of kings; at that moment he had a divine body and was seated in a divine vehicle,
an umbrella held over him, fanned by hosts of apsarases, clad in divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Calling out to his wife from above, he went to his own city: "Come quickly, fortunate one; you will be my wife."
Honoured with praise by siddhas, vidyadharas and yakshas, a shower of flowers arranged by the king of the gods fell from on high.
Meanwhile, O king, he spoke again to his wife: "You were cursed by the great-souled Chyavana for the sake of your daughter.
Release yourself and reach the abode of those who walk in dharma." Reminded thus by the voice from the sky, the king went to his city.
Taking her sons, she came and said to her husband: "Whatever the goal of my husband, that will always be mine."
Her husband said: "Quickly enter the fire. At the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday, at the confluence of the Erandi holy place,
the bone that fell there will carry you across sin." Saying "So be it" to him, the female bird then quickly
gathered grass and wood and kindled a fire; then she mounted her husband's vehicle together with her sons.
As Uma has Maheshvara and as Rama has the lord of Shri, so she obtained her husband by the power of this holy place.
Having thus mounted the vehicle with his wife, the king then — Chandrasena, Devasena and Yajnasena too —
surrounded by his three sons, devoted to righteous conduct, entered the lovely city of Ayodhya, built by the gods,
filled with supreme joy, with his women and retinue; having ruled for a hundred thousand years, he then reached Shiva's abode.
Having worshipped Erandishvara at the confluence of the Erandi, O king, eighty-five thousand great-souled kshatriyas
went there, king of kings, truly to Shambhu's city. This I have told you, O king, this ancient story;
by hearing or reciting it one gains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Having performed the horse sacrifice, the best of rites, at the confluence of the Erandi, you will give the merit of all sacrifices to the brahmin.
Having said this to Suryasena, he went to Shiva's abode. Saying "So be it" to him, the valorous Suryasena,
having reflected thus in his mind, furnished with all materials, the lord of the earth went with the gods, taking the maiden.
Then the king made pavilions and sacrificial posts five yojanas in extent, remembering his father's command.
The sacrifice was begun by him and completed with excellent fees. Sukanya, the king's sister, playing with the maidens,
hearing a sound in an anthill, came to play there; there she saw a man, eyeless, face downward.
Seeing him, she pierced him with a thorn and went home. There was a great outcry: "What is this?", O Bharata.
Suryasena, dejected, quickly summoned with the brahmins the two gods, the Ashvins, and the chastiser of Paka,
and duly completed the sacrifice according to rule. Having completed the sacrifice, the supremely righteous king
entreated the gods: "Give the great-souled Chyavana divine sight, a lovely body and fresh youth."
Thus entreated, the gods gave sight, Yudhishthira, and a body endowed with beauty and youth, like that of Kamadeva.
Then, having appeased Chyavana, he said: "Forgive, fortunate one, what Sukanya did to you;
take her hand, O sage, and give up your anger." Entreated thus by the king, the sage said "Om."
Then at the concluding bath, at the confluence of the Chandavega, having duly set up the couple and given him the fruit of the sacrifice,
the king performed the charming wedding of Sukanya; the two, bearing divine forms like Lakshmi and Narayana,
became husband and wife there, their eyes wide with joy. Having given the maiden to the sage there, Suryasena went to his city
and enjoyed many pleasures, valorous as Shakra. Whoever at the end of a meal remembers Suryasena, Sukanya, Chyavana, Shakra and the Ashvins
does not lose his sight. This I have told you, O king, of the confluence of the Chanda and the Erandaka;
bathing there one goes to heaven and does not enter a womb again; one should sacrifice with the horse sacrifice or release a blue bull.
I shall tell a story as seen and heard. Durvasas, the fierce ascetic, wandered through all the holy places;
coming to Pitritirtha for the good of the ancestors, bathing there and worshipping the trident-bearer and the Grandsire,
he offered handfuls of water with kusha and sesame and the ancestral pinda. Having given the pinda, he said to the sages, filled with great wonder:
I have heard that here the ancestors take the pindas in their hands; today I do not see that — the pilgrimage is pointless.
Knowing him to be a fierce ascetic, the sages then said: "The ancestors take in their hands the pinda offered on the new-moon day;
this is true, best of sages, not otherwise — it is spoken by the Veda. Wait for that new moon, wishing to see other holy places."
Then the brahmin sage grew angry and said: "I will not offer the pinda here, nor bathe nor give gifts."
Then Durvasas said to Eranda, the eminent sage, the great sage holding a water-pot full of water in his hand:

Why do you torment your body? Your austerity here is fruitless. Take a single water-pot and go to Omkara and the Kalpaga.
skandapuran:44:33	The one Grandsire, the imperishable lord, is to be worshipped at Gaya. Having said this, with the sages, to the mountain Amarakantaka
the greatly radiant one came, and going there, O Bharata, having worshipped Omkara, he uttered this hymn:
Hearing this divine hymn, Shiva bearing the form of Omkara said: "Choose a boon, fortunate one."
Durvasas said: "If you are pleased, lord of gods, if a boon is to be given me, grant me that this holy place be equal to Pitritirtha."
Omkara said: "Let all this be so today by my grace, rich in austerity; even the impossible is possible for you in the three worlds with the moving and unmoving."
Having thus obtained the boon, the brahmin Durvasas, the fierce ascetic, dwelt with the sages on the eastern side of the mountain.
Meanwhile, best of kings, Narada said to Brahma: "The Pitritirtha of Gaya has perished through the anger of Durvasas;
he dwells on the bank of the Narmada at Omkara at Amarakantaka." Hearing Narada's words, Brahma, out of compassion for the worlds,
mounting his swan vehicle with the gods, best of kings, came to the hermitage there where Durvasas dwelt.
Seeing the god Grandsire, Eranda, the eminent sage, taking his water-pot, at the feet of Brahma
poured it out as is right, gave arghya and stood; the stream that arose from the water-pot's water went to the Narmada.
Then Durvasas duly worshipped the Grandsire. Brahma said: "If a holy place is to arise for you at the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday —
now the Pitritirtha is not seen here by people. Your curse cannot be turned back; fulfil it now."
Durvasas said: "The curse has been withdrawn by me at your word, Grandsire. The sight of the ancestors there, which releases the ancestors of Gaya,
will come about by your grace at that holy place, Grandsire." Saying "So be it" to him, Brahma went to heaven, O king,
having bowed to Maheshana, saluted by gods and asuras, filled with great joy, honoured by excellent brahmins.
Durvasas, best of sages, vanished right there. Therefore the Erandi, which came there, is most holy in the world.
The Erandishvara linga, saluted by gods and asuras — one of meritorious deeds should see it at the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday.
Having seen that supreme linga, one does not see Yama's world. This I have told you, O king, O Bharata;
by hearing and reciting it one goes to Maheshvara's city.
There was a king named Bharata in the solar line, lord of the people; he ruled the whole earth, great king.
As far as grass is known and as far as the sun's fame extends, so far is the land of Bharata, with its mountains, forests and woods.
Once that best of kings, devoted to the rite of sacrifice, to the south of Bhrigu made a sacrificial ground adorned with fire-pits and pavilions,
ten yojanas in extent. Ten lakh milch cows with their calves,
one lakh horses and ten thousand elephants, gems, rubies and jewels, and garments of many kinds —
taking the implements of sacrifice, furnished with all materials, touching heaven and earth with the sound of Vedic recitation,
the gods dwelling in the seven worlds were satisfied by the oblation. When the sacrifice of that king of boundless radiance was thus under way,
to destroy the sacrifice came rakshasas of fierce form — Malyavan, Sumali, Sukeshi, Shankha and Dushana —
thousands of rakshasas came quickly; the dreadful ones broke the things of the sacrifice, terrible in the three worlds.
All the gods fled and the officiating priests were struck down. When the sacrifice had thus been destroyed by the rakshasas, sinless one,
the king blazed with anger like fire fed with oblation, and slew all the rakshasas as the wielder of the thunderbolt the mountains.
Seeing the brahmins and officiating priests who had fled in fear, fallen on the ground, slain by the rakshasas,
Bharata, overcome by grief, then said to the counsellor of the gods: "You are the guru of all the gods, knower of the three times and the three Vedas.
The sin of killing brahmins and the like has come about on my account through the thorns of the gods; what expiation must I perform? Tell me, Brihaspati."
Brihaspati said: "I give you the knowledge of reviving the dead, best of kings." The brahmins and gods, revived, praised the counsellor of the gods.
Then the sacrifice was completed with full excellent fees. Arising from the root of the sacrificial post, the Shalya and Vishalyaka
entered, great king, the Narmada, purifier of the world. Then the gods, mounting each his own vehicle, went to heaven,
and Bharata too entered his city with the brahmins. Thus the Shalya and Vishalya are renowned in the three worlds,
and the Bharateshvara linga stands at Brahmayoni. This I have told you, O king, as seen and as heard;
by hearing and reciting it one does not enter the straits of the womb.
Likewise seven others are indicated, the excellent stairway to heaven; Bhairava, best of Bhrigus, is to be known at Amarakantaka.
Shudras, kshatriyas, vaishyas, outcastes and the lowly give up their lives there, except the brahmin, O king;
a brahmin who falls there becomes a slayer of a brahmin and a self-slayer.
At the conjunction of Rahu and Soma one becomes a king in the city of the vidyadharas for twenty-two thousand years, O king.
When the sun is seized by Rahu one enjoys double fruit. Whoever, helplessly or willingly, struck by flood of water or by fire,
dies having reached Bhrigu becomes king of the vidyadharas. Bhrigu, in the form of Bhairava, is like the Vindhya and Kailasa.
Those who revile Bhrigu split the linga and Brahman; Bhairava does not forgive them, so Skanda declared.
A brahmin fallen from renunciation, a matricide and patricide, one who goes to his sister, his daughter-in-law or his own kinswoman —
for these, falling is commended, or purification in a fire of dried dung; by that he is freed from that sin and goes to Shiva's world.
At Harishchandrapura, at Chandra, at Shrishaila near Tripurantaka, at Traiyambaka, Dhautapapa, and the Varaha of the Vindhya,
and likewise at the pool of the Kaveri, by falling one attains heaven. To the south of Bhrigu is the linga Chapaleshvara,
renowned here as protector of the field, destroyer of sin; the field of Chapaleshvara is to be known as sixty bow-lengths.
The man who climbs the mountain without seeing it — he takes away all the fruit of his merit, no doubt.
Having painted the sun on a cloth adorned with a banner-staff, wearing a bracelet on his hand, fanned with chowries,
the hero should go to fall and climb the Bhrigu mountain; at every step he gains the fruit of a sacrifice, so Shankara said.
Apsarases bewitched by love always wait there, mounted on divine vehicles, adorned with divine ornaments.
The hero who falls there, leaving his own body, at once has a divine body, valorous as Shakra;
mounting a vehicle that grants desires, amid the apsarases vying with one another, he goes to Shiva's city accompanied by them.
